addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

attachment.content:
- graphify: Use for any question about a codebase, its architecture, file relationships, or project content — especially when graphify-out/ exists, where the question should be treated as a graphify query first. Turns any input (code, docs, papers, images, videos) into a persistent knowledge graph with god nodes, community detection, and query/path/explain tools.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.prompt:
I need to trace how a browser request for another user's profile image (avatar) is served in this codebase — from the HTTP route handler all the way down to the data/storage layer. 

Search very thoroughly for:
1. Routes or handlers related to serving user profile images / avatars (look for URL patterns like /avatar, /profile/image, /user/*/avatar, etc.)
2. The handler function that processes these requests
3. Any service/business logic layer it calls
4. Any data access / storage layer it reaches (database queries, file system reads, S3/blob storage access, etc.)

Look in router files, handler files, service files, repository/store files. Check for terms like "avatar", "profile image", "profile picture", "photo", "user image". Also check for image serving, static file serving related to user content.

Report each hop: the function/method name, the file path, and what it does. Be very thorough — check multiple naming conventions.

content.text: I now have the complete end-to-end trace. Here is the full report. --- ## End-to-End Trace: Serving a User's Avatar Image This is a Go (Memos) application using the Echo HTTP framework. The avatar is stored as a base64-encoded data URI in the database's `avatar_url` column on the `user` table. There is no separate file/blob storage for avatars -- the image data is inline in the database row itself. ### Hop 0: Frontend initiates the request **File:** `/bench/home/work/web/src/components/UserAvatar.tsx` **Component:** `UserAvatar` The `` tag sets its `src` to the `avatarUrl` prop. When the API returns user data, the converter on the server rewrites base64 data URIs to a path like `/file/users/{username}/avatar` (see Hop 1b below), so the browser issues a `GET /file/users/{username}/avatar` request. ### Hop 1a: API returns the rewritten avatar URL (how the browser learns the URL) **File:** `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/user_service_converters.go` **Function:** `convertUserFromStore(user *store.User, viewer *store.User) *v1pb.User` (line 16) When the gRPC/REST API serializes a `User` for any response (GetUser, ListUsers, BatchGetUsers, etc.), this converter checks if `user.AvatarURL` is a base64 data URI. If it is, the converter replaces it with a relative URL: ```go userpb.AvatarUrl = fmt.Sprintf("/file/%s/avatar", userpb.Name) // e.g. "/file/users/steven/avatar" ``` If the avatar URL is already an external URL (not a data URI), it is passed through unchanged. This ensures the API never returns a multi-megabyte base64 blob in JSON responses. ### Hop 1b: Route registration **File:** `/bench/home/work/server/server.go` **Function:** `NewServer(...)` (line 44) At server startup (line 81-82): ```go fileServerService := fileserver.NewFileServerService(s.Profile, s.Store, s.Secret) fileServerService.RegisterRoutes(echoServer) ``` **File:** `/bench/home/work/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go` **Function:** `RegisterRoutes(echoServer *echo.Echo)` (line 121) Registers the route (line 124): ```go fileGroup.GET("/users/:identifier/avatar", s.serveUserAvatar) ``` This means the full URL pattern is `GET /file/users/:identifier/avatar`. ### Hop 2: HTTP handler -- `serveUserAvatar` **File:** `/bench/home/work/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go` **Function:** `serveUserAvatar(c *echo.Context) error` (line 167) This is the entry point for the avatar request. It performs these steps in order: 1. **Authentication check (lines 173-181):** If the instance is private (no `InstanceURL` configured, checked via `s.Profile.AllowAnonymous()`), it requires a valid session. It calls `s.getCurrentUser(ctx, c)` which delegates to the `Authenticator`. 2. **Resolve the target user (lines 183-191):** Extracts the `:identifier` path parameter (which is a username) and calls `s.getUserByUsername(ctx, identifier)`. 3. **Check avatar existence (lines 192-194):** If `user.AvatarURL` is empty, returns 404. 4. **Parse the data URI (line 196):** Calls `s.parseDataURI(user.AvatarURL)` which uses a regex to extract the MIME type and base64-decode the image bytes from the `data:image/png;base64,...` string. 5. **Validate MIME type (lines 201-203):** Checks the image type against `avatarAllowedTypes` (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, HEIC, HEIF). 6. **Set security and cache headers (lines 205-207):** Sets `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Content-Security-Policy`, `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600`. 7. **Return the image bytes (line 209):** Sends the decoded binary image data with the appropriate Content-Type. ### Hop 3: Authentication -- `getCurrentUser` **File:** `/bench/home/work/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go` **Function:** `getCurrentUser(ctx, c)` (line 708) Extracts the `Authorization` header and `Cookie` header, then delegates to: **File:** `/bench/home/work/server/auth/authenticator.go` **Function:** `AuthenticateToUser(ctx, authHeader, cookieHeader)` (line 190) This tries authentication in order: 1. **Bearer token** (access token v2 or Personal Access Token) via `resolveBearer` (line 149) 2. **Refresh token cookie** fallback via `AuthenticateByRefreshToken` (line 61) Returns `(*store.User, nil)` on success, or `(nil, nil)` if no valid credentials. ### Hop 4: User lookup -- `getUserByUsername` **File:** `/bench/home/work/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go` **Function:** `getUserByUsername(ctx, identifier)` (line 715) Calls: ```go return s.Store.GetUser(ctx, &store.FindUser{Username: &identifier}) ``` ### Hop 5: Store layer -- `Store.GetUser` **File:** `/bench/home/work/store/user.go` **Function:** `GetUser(ctx, find *FindUser) (*User, error)` (line 148) 1. If `find.ID` is set, checks the in-memory cache (`s.userCache`) first. For username-based lookups (as in the avatar flow), the cache is not hit directly. 2. Delegates to `s.ListUsers(ctx, find)` (line 158). 3. Returns the first result (or nil if none found). ### Hop 6: Store layer -- `Store.ListUsers` **File:** `/bench/home/work/store/user.go` **Function:** `ListUsers(ctx, find *FindUser) ([]*User, error)` (line 136) Delegates to the database driver: ```go list, err := s.driver.ListUsers(ctx, find) ``` Then populates the user cache for each returned user. ### Hop 7: Database driver -- `DB.ListUsers` (SQLite example) **File:** `/bench/home/work/store/db/sqlite/user.go` **Function:** `ListUsers(ctx, find *store.FindUser) ([]*store.User, error)` (line 88) Builds and executes a SQL query against the `user` table. The query selects these columns (lines 152-163): ```sql SELECT id, username, role, email, nickname, password_hash, avatar_url, description, created_ts, updated_ts, row_status FROM user WHERE username = ? ORDER BY created_ts DESC, row_status DESC, id DESC ``` The `avatar_url` column (line 159) is scanned into `user.AvatarURL` (line 189). This column contains the full base64-encoded data URI string (e.g., `data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo...`). Equivalent drivers exist for MySQL (`/bench/home/work/store/db/mysql/user.go`) and PostgreSQL (`/bench/home/work/store/db/postgres/user.go`). ### Hop 8: Data URI parsing -- `parseDataURI` **File:** `/bench/home/work/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go` **Function:** `parseDataURI(dataURI string) (string, []byte, error)` (line 737) Uses the regex `^data:(?P[^;]+);base64,(?P.+)` (line 98) to extract: - The MIME type (e.g., `image/png`) - The base64 payload, which it decodes with `base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString` Returns the MIME type string and the raw image bytes. --- ### Summary of the complete call chain ``` Browser GET /file/users/{username}/avatar | v [fileserver.go] serveUserAvatar() -- HTTP handler | +---> [fileserver.go] getCurrentUser() -- auth check (private instances only) | +---> [authenticator.go] AuthenticateToUser() | +---> resolveBearer() or AuthenticateByRefreshToken() | +---> [fileserver.go] getUserByUsername() -- look up the target user | +---> [user.go] Store.GetUser() | +---> [user.go] Store.ListUsers() | +---> [sqlite/user.go] DB.ListUsers() | +---> SQL: SELECT ... avatar_url ... FROM user WHERE username = ? | +---> [fileserver.go] parseDataURI() -- decode base64 data URI from DB column | +---> avatarAllowedTypes check -- MIME type validation | +---> c.Blob(200, imageType, imageData) -- send raw image bytes to browser ``` ### Key architectural observations - **No separate file/blob storage for avatars.** Unlike attachments (which support local filesystem, S3, and database blob storage), avatars are stored entirely as base64-encoded data URIs in the `avatar_url` text column of the `user` database table. - **The API never returns raw base64 in JSON.** The `convertUserFromStore` converter rewrites data URI values to `/file/users/{username}/avatar` paths so clients fetch the image via a separate HTTP request. - **Caching.** The store has an in-memory cache (`userCache` with 10-minute TTL, max 1000 items) that caches `User` objects by ID. The HTTP response includes `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` for browser caching. - **Security.** Avatar MIME types are validated at both upload time (in `UpdateUser`, lines 335-351 of `user_service.go`) and serving time (line 201 of `fileserver.go`). Security headers (`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, CSP) are set on every response. - **Privacy.** On a private instance (no `InstanceURL`), anonymous visitors cannot access avatars -- authentication is required (lines 173-181).

content.text:
h07.

Tracing `GET /file/users/:identifier/avatar` from the browser to stored data:

`serveUserAvatar` — `server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go`
`getCurrentUser` — `server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go`
`AuthenticateToUser` — `server/auth/authenticator.go`
`getUserByUsername` — `server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go`
`Store.GetUser` — `store/user.go`
`Store.ListUsers` — `store/user.go`
`driver.ListUsers` — `store/db/sqlite/user.go` (or `mysql/user.go`, `postgres/user.go`)
`parseDataURI` — `server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go`

The route is registered in `server/server.go` where `FileServerService.RegisterRoutes` mounts the Echo group, and in `fileserver.go` at `fileGroup.GET("/users/:identifier/avatar", s.serveUserAvatar)`.

The handler authenticates the request (on private instances), resolves the username to a `store.User` via `GetUser` → `ListUsers` → the DB driver's `ListUsers` which runs `SELECT … avatar_url … FROM user WHERE username = ?`. The `avatar_url` column holds a base64 data URI (`data:image/png;base64,…`). Back in the handler, `parseDataURI` decodes it into raw bytes and MIME type, which are returned to the browser via `c.Blob()`. The API never sends the base64 blob inline in JSON — `convertUserFromStore` in `server/router/api/v1/user_service_converters.go` rewrites it to the `/file/users/{username}/avatar` path so the browser fetches the image separately.
